rationale: For the symbolic use presented in the entry, the book gives the stronger explanation of the focal evidence. Ezekiel 31 explicitly identifies the great trees with imperial rulers and their peoples: Assyria is a cedar, while the concluding identification is “Pharaoh and all his multitude.” Placing such nation-trees together among “the trees of Eden” in “the garden of God” supports the compositional inference that the garden is an arranged collection of peoples or nations. God’s statement “I have made him fair,” together with the planting and felling imagery in Ezekiel 17 and Daniel 4, supports the gardener’s governing role. The paradise/divine-presence reading remains compelling for Eden and the wider canonical motif, but in Ezekiel 31 it does not explain as precisely why the garden’s individual trees represent comparable imperial bodies that envy, flourish, and fall. The entry should be understood as a symbolic glossary identification, not as a denial that many biblical gardens are literal locations or carry paradise imagery.
book_core_identification: A garden symbolically represents a grouping of nations or peoples, derived from its constituent trees representing rulers, houses, or national bodies.
book_secondary_elaborations: The grouping is planted or deliberately arranged.
The grouped peoples stand under a gardener’s rule.
chapter_only_objections: The extension of the garden symbol to Isaiah’s garden-cult passages is disputable; literal pagan groves or cultic gardens remain a strong contextual reading.
The interpretation of Isaiah 66:17 as primarily describing participation in foreign nations rather than cultic conduct is not necessary to establish the glossary entry.
The chapter’s conclusion that clean-food restrictions remain eternally binding is a separate theological claim and is not established by the glossary definition.
The book’s broader methodological demand that symbols hold uniformly across Scripture may overstate how consistently imagery functions across different genres and contexts.
strongest_counter_interpretation: A garden primarily signifies a divinely ordered realm of abundant life and divine presence—paradise—while Ezekiel 31 merely places metaphorical empire-trees inside Edenic scenery to emphasize their extraordinary glory and subsequent humiliation; the garden itself does not independently symbolize a federation or grouping of nations.
counter_core_identification: Garden is paradise or a divinely cultivated realm of flourishing life and presence, not a symbolic grouping of peoples.
material_core_denial: The counter-reading denies that the garden’s constituent-tree structure carries a corporate political meaning, treating the nation-trees as comparisons placed within an Edenic setting instead.
counter_case: Genesis 2–3 directly presents Eden as a divinely planted place of life, provision, vocation, and lost access rather than as an assembly of nations.
Isaiah 51:3 and Ezekiel 36:35 use Eden or the LORD’s garden as an image of restored fertility and blessedness.
Revelation 2:7 and 22:1–5 reuse Edenic tree-and-river imagery to portray restored life in God’s presence.
In Ezekiel 31, “garden of God” can function as the superlative setting in which magnificent rulers are compared with Eden’s trees, without making “garden” a fixed code for nations.
book_explanatory_advantages: It accounts for Ezekiel 31’s explicit movement from individual trees to Assyria, Pharaoh, and their corporate multitudes.
It explains why several comparable trees can envy one another and undergo political exaltation or judgment.
Daniel 4 independently establishes a great tree as a king together with his dominion, while Ezekiel 17 connects planted and felled trees with royal houses and God’s sovereignty.
The ordinary compositional relation between a garden and its trees provides a straightforward mechanism: if the trees are national bodies, their planted collective is a grouping of such bodies.
The phrase “garden of God” and God’s declaration “I have made him fair” support divine cultivation and rule.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It better captures the dominant function of garden imagery in Genesis, restoration prophecies, and Revelation.
It preserves the Edenic force of Ezekiel’s wording without requiring “garden” to possess a uniform political-symbolic meaning.
It accommodates context-specific uses in the Song of Songs, Gethsemane, and the garden tomb more naturally than a universal nations-and-peoples definition.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 31:3, 9, 18: Assyria and Pharaoh with his multitude are represented through trees placed among the trees of Eden in God’s garden.
Daniel 4:10–23: the great tree is explicitly decoded as Nebuchadnezzar together with his far-reaching dominion.
Ezekiel 17:22–24: God plants, exalts, dries, and flourishes royal and national trees, supporting the gardener-rule element.
unresolved_objections: The entry is too compressed to state explicitly that this is a contextual symbolic sense rather than the exhaustive meaning of every biblical garden.
The inference from multiple nation-trees to the garden itself as a grouping of nations is compositional rather than an explicit biblical gloss saying “the garden is the nations.”
The paradise/divine-presence interpretation remains superior for many garden passages outside the focal prophetic symbolism.
